extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/early-graduate students and readers of algebraic number theory (Math 361 level)
extracted.subtask_description: An undergraduate-level expository project that develops the theory of binary quadratic forms and imaginary quadratic fields to explain Gauss' class number problems and the complete determination of imaginary quadratic fields with class number one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of binary quadratic forms and discriminant
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary quadratic forms are expressions ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 for a,b,c ∈ Z. The discriminant of the form is d = b^2 − 4ac.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus primarily on forms with negative discriminant (d < 0). Distinguish primitive forms (gcd(a,b,c)=1), positive-definite (f(x,y) ≥ 0 for all (x,y)), negative-definite, and indefinite. Fundamental discriminants are those with d ≡ 1 (mod 4) square-free or d = 4n with n ≡ 2,3 (mod 4) square-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of forms via GL2(Z) and proper equivalence via SL2(Z)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms f(x,y) and g(x,y) are equivalent if there exists M = [[p,q],[r,s]] ∈ GL2(Z) with ps − qr = ±1 such that f(x,y) = g(px+qy, rx+sy). The equivalence is proper if M ∈ SL2(Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence is an equivalence relation induced by the group action of GL2(Z) (or SL2(Z) for proper equivalence) on forms; classes are the orbits under this action and proper classes are orbits under SL2(Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant: equivalent forms have same discriminant
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: Any two equivalent forms have the same discriminant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via expressing coefficients of one form in terms of the other using the change-of-variables matrix and showing b^2 − 4ac = (ps − qr)^2(B^2 − 4AC), hence discriminants agree when det=±1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced form notion and bounds on coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: A form is reduced if |b| ≤ a ≤ c and b ≥ 0 when a = |b| or a = c. Every primitive positive-definite form is properly equivalent to a unique reduced form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reduction to enumerate classes; bounds like |b| ≤ a ≤ sqrt(−d/3) (derived from −d = 4ac − b^2 ≥ 3a^2) give a finite search space of reduced forms for fixed discriminant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and finiteness of the class number h(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class number h(d) is the number of inequivalent primitive positive-definite forms of discriminant d (equivalently number of reduced forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem: for fixed d the number h(d) is finite; this follows from the bound on coefficients and reduction theory (each proper equivalence class contains a unique reduced form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauss' class number problem (general statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given n, determine all discriminants d such that h(d) = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem splits into subquestions (e.g., showing lim_{d→−∞} h(d) = ∞; classifying d with h(d)=1; determining d with small h(d)). The paper highlights the special case n=1 (class number one problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Landau's theorem for even discriminants (criterion for h(−4n)=1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Landau: For positive integer n, h(−4n) = 1 if and only if n ∈ {1,2,3,4,7}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: for each possible n not in the set, construct another reduced form of discriminant −4n not equivalent to x^2 + ny^2 (by casework: n not a prime power; n a power of 2; n a power of an odd prime), thus showing h(−4n) > 1. Use explicit coefficient arguments and small-case computations (and computer checks for some cases like n=31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic enumeration of reduced forms (computational method)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can compute all primitive reduced forms of a given discriminant via a routine that searches coefficients within the derived bounds and tests reduction/equivalence; the class number is the length of the list of reduced forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author implements a Python function findForm that prints tuples (a,b,c) for each primitive reduced form; this is feasible for modest discriminants and essential for large ones (example: 52 reduced forms for discriminant −32767).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence: fundamental discriminants ↔ quadratic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A discriminant d is a fundamental discriminant of a form iff d is the discriminant of a quadratic field K; there is exactly one quadratic field (up to isomorphism) for each fundamental discriminant (d ≠ 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification justifies shifting from form-class perspective to quadratic-field perspective for the class number problem and motivates restricting attention to fundamental discriminants (imaginary quadratic fields when d < 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal class group and field class number h_K
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadratic field K, the ideal class group C_K = {fractional ideals}/{principal fractional ideals}; the class number h_K is the order of C_K. h_K = 1 iff O_K is a PID (equivalently a UFD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding ideals and principal fractional ideals is necessary to translate form-class results into algebraic number theory statements about when rings of integers are PIDs/UFDs (e.g., relation to prime-producing polynomials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism between form class group and ideal class group
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem: For imaginary quadratic field K of discriminant d < 0, the homomorphism φ: C(d) → C_K sending ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 to the ideal (a, (−b + √d)/2) is an isomorphism; hence h(d) = h_K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem is the bridge that allows computation in the classical form language to determine algebraic properties of quadratic fields; use either side depending on convenience for computation or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of class number as d → −∞ (historical criterion/result)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class number h(d) tends to infinity as d → −∞ (Heilbronn's theorem), established by combining results of Hecke, Deuring, Mordell, and Heilbronn with logical arguments independent of the truth of the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof methods are non-effective and do not describe the exact rate of divergence; the result removes the possibility of boundedness of h(d) for large negative discriminants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baker-Heegner-Stark theorem (complete determination of class number one)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are exactly nine fundamental discriminants d < 0 for which h(d) = 1: d = −3, −4, −7, −8, −11, −19, −43, −67, −163.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: even discriminants handled by Landau; odd discriminants reduced to d = −p (p ≡ 3 mod 4) and then studied via modular functions (j-function), yielding Diophantine equations whose solutions give the remaining values. Heegner's original work, later confirmed/corrected by Baker and Stark, produces the complete list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reductions for checking h(d)=1 in odd cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering d ≡ 1 (mod 4) with h(d)=1, one can reduce to d = −p where p ≡ 3 (mod 4) is prime; further congruence information (p modulo 8) influences the argument (e.g., p ≡ 7 (mod 8) forces p = 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For p ≡ 3 (mod 8) the methods become more intricate, invoking modular forms and the j-function to obtain explicit polynomial/Diophantine constraints; this is the pathway used by Heegner/Stark/Baker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of explicit tables/data as evidence and check
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabulated reduced forms for discriminants (e.g., Table 1 listing reduced forms of discriminant −4n and their class numbers) provide concrete checks of theoretical claims and are useful for small discriminants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine theoretical reductions with explicit computation (by hand or program) to confirm completeness of lists (e.g., Landau's set) and to handle exceptional small cases.
